title: ESP32 UART 0 changing the baudrate
body:
I am in the process of writing a replacement file manger for an ESP32 running MicroPython. The new file manager will be cross platform but for the time being I am working on getting it up and running on Windows. Th file manager I am writing leverages the Windows API using a kernel mode driver so the ESP32 will be seen as a removable drive to the OS. This has a slew of benefits like in place file editing and drag and drop using the OS's file manager. IDE's will be able to access the device directly. It will function the same way when I add Linux support to it.

Now that you know what I am doing this is the problem I am having..

using a 115200 bitrate to communicate over is simply not going to cut it. I need to bump that bitrate up to 460800. I also need to get rid of using the repl and sending python command over it to carry out tasks. This simply has to much overhead and I am not able to use multiple threads on the ESP32 very easily. I need to be able to send byte data to instruct the program on the ESP32.

How the file manager works is it backup up the current boot.py file and replace it with one that I made and contains all the relevant code needed for it to work. when the esp32 gets ejected/unmounted the program will place the original boot.py file back into place.

My issues are 

* I am not able to set the bitrate on UART 0. 
* UART 0 always gets bound to the repl

this is the default boot.py file and there are no lines in it that set the repl to UART 0 using uos.dupterm.
```python
# This file is executed on every boot (including wake-boot from deepsleep)
# import esp
# esp.osdebug(None)
# import webrepl
# webrepl.start()
```
has this been removed for some reason? and if so why????

comments.author: participant6
comments.body:
Sorry, to comment on an issue that's been closed for some time now but it seems the most direct way to contact people like @reporter who seem to have got the changes introduced in commit 919e586 to work for them. Sorry that the following comment is so long but I wanted to show I'd "done my homework" and also wanted to provide information for anyone else who runs across this issue.

First off - I have been able to change the baud rate for UART0 but things don't work quite as I expect.

The first issue is essentially cosmetic. I'm assuming I can only change the baud rate for UART0 by creating a new `machine.UART` instance that corresponds to it. I.e. there's no way to retrieve an existing `UART` instance, e.g. by doing something like:

```
uart0 = os.dupterm(None, 0)
```

`dupterm` just returns `None`.

OK. So, I create a new instance like this (leaving all the characteristics of the UART unchanged in this first step):

```
from machine import UART

UART(0)
```

This works, but creating the `UART` instance always results in:

```
E (738) uart: uart_wait_tx_done(1115): uart driver error
```

However, this appears to be cosmetic as this little program successfully changes the baud rate to 9600:

```
import os
import sys
import time
import micropython

from machine import UART

# Give myself a chance to bail and upload a new program.
print('Press ctrl-C now to exit')
time.sleep(3)
print("Taking control of the USB UART")
time.sleep_ms(200)

os.dupterm(None, 0)
UART(0, 9600, timeout=0)

buffer = memoryview(bytearray(1024))

micropython.kbd_intr(-1)

while True:
    read_count = sys.stdin.buffer.readinto(buffer[:1])
    if read_count is not None and read_count > 0:
        sys.stdout.buffer.write(buffer[:read_count])
    else:
        sys.stdout.buffer.write(b'.')
```

So, there are a couple of problems:

* As I'd set `timeout` to 0, I had hoped I'd see a stream of `.` characters when there wasn't anything to read but the `readinto` is blocking and I can't find any way to make it non-blocking.
* You don't see the `uart driver error` in this situation (I presume it somehow becomes "invisible" to `mpremote` in REPL mode due to the change in baud rate). But you see it e.g. if you use a terminal emulator, like the UNIX `screen` command, that, unlike `mpremote`, can be started with the baud rate set to 9600 and you then press the boards reset button:

```
$ screen /dev/ttyUSB0 9600
��B�����J1�9� �m�����h�ښ�j�(3769) uart: uart_wait_tx_done(1115): uart driver error
```

The initial bytes of jibberish are just the initial output after I pressed the reset button and things are still using 115200 baud.

I can get around the blocking issue like so using `select.poll`:

```
poller = select.poll()
poller.register(sys.stdin.buffer, select.POLLIN | select.POLLERR | select.POLLHUP)

while True:
    for (s, event) in poller.ipoll(0):
        if event != select.POLLIN:
            print(f"got unexprected event {event}")
        else:
            read_count = s.readinto(buffer[:1])
            if read_count is not None and read_count > 0:
                b = buffer[0]
                if b < b' '[0] or b > b'~'[0]:
                    print("?")
                else:
                    print(str(b))
            else:
                print("failed to write character")
```

But the `readinto` is still blocking so, I can only read one byte at a time, using `ipoll` to essentially tell me "yes, there's at least one byte available so you won't block if you call `readinto` for a single byte".

Really, I'd like to read as many bytes as are available in one go without blocking but I don't think I can get a byte count using `ipoll` and I don't see an equivalent of `UART.any()`.

That brings me to my final point - the above does get me where I want (despite the apparently harmless `uart driver error` when creating the `UART` instance).

But I had actually been hoping I could use the `UART` instance I'd created rather than having to work through `sys.stdin` and `sys.stdout`. But while creating the `UART` has achieved something - changing the baud rate of UART0 - the resulting `UART` instance doesn't seem to be useable. In the following program, I get:

**1.** `uart: uart_wait_tx_done(1115): uart driver error` on creating the `UART` (as before this seems to be harmless).
**2.** More lethally, when I call `uart.any()`, I get:

> ```
> E (3979) uart: uart_get_buffered_data_len(1340): uart driver error
> Traceback (most recent call last):
>   File "main.py", line 18, in <module>
> OSError: [Errno 1] EPERM: ESP_FAIL
> ```

```
import os
import time

from machine import UART

# Give myself a chance to bail and upload a new program.
print('Press ctrl-C now to exit')
time.sleep(3)
print("Taking control of the USB UART")
time.sleep_ms(200)

os.dupterm(None, 0)
uart = UART(0, baudrate=9600, timeout=0)

buffer = memoryview(bytearray(1024))

while True:
    available = uart.any()
    if available > 0:
        read_count = uart.readinto(buffer[:available])
        if read_count is not None and read_count > 0:
            write_count = uart.write(buffer[:read_count])
            if write_count != read_count:
                uart.write(b'?')
```

If I simply call `uart.write(b'?')`, it doesn't work either but it's not as lethal as calling `uart.any()`, it results in an error but doesn't terminate the program:

```
E (3959) uart: uart_write_bytes(1245): uart driver error
```

comments.author: participant6
comments.body:
Thanks for your reply, Kevin 👍 

When MicroPython and its REPL start-up, the UART associated with stdin and stdout only exists at the C level underlying the ESP32 MicroPython implementation.

Creating a `machine.UART` instance corresponding to UART0 (as you've done in `boot.py` and I've done in my examples) doesn't currently create a valid `machine.UART` object that can then be used directly in ones code. Instead, calling the `machine.UART` constructor for UART0 essentially just communicates a set of changes to its configuration (such as baud rate) to the underlying C code (which is then reflected in how stdin and stderr behave).

I wish I knew if this was deliberate when @participant11 made his changes in commit 919e586, i.e. that it's just about communicating configuration changes to the C level and not about creating a valid `machine.UART` object that one can interact with in ones MicroPython code. If so, fair enough, I'm just hoping for some clarity.

So, in summary, I'm curious to find out:

1. Is it expected that the resulting `machine.UART` instance should be unusable in terms of interacting with it in MicroPython code?
2. If one must instead work with stdin/stdout, can one use stdin in a non-blocking manner? Or is there an equivalent of [`machine.UART.any()`](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/library/machine.UART.html#machine.UART.any). Posts like this [one](https://forum.micropython.org/viewtopic.php?t=12162) seem to suggest the best one can do is a poll and read **per** character (rather than a non-blocking read of as many as are currently available). 
3. Least important - what's causing the apparently harmless error `(3769) uart: uart_wait_tx_done(1115): uart driver error` when one creates a `machine.UART` instance corresponding to UART0.

Minimal examples of each issue...

**1.** Created `machine.UART` UART0 instance is not directly useable in MicroPython code:

```
import os

uart = UART(0, baudrate=9600, timeout=0)

uart.write(b'.')  # Results in `uart_write_bytes` error`.
uart.any()  # Results in `uart_get_buffered_data_len` error and exception `OSError: [Errno 1] EPERM: ESP_FAIL`.
```

**2.** Best equivalent of a non-blocking read is `poll`/`ipoll` and reading _a byte at a time_:

```
import os
import sys

from machine import UART

UART(0, 9600, timeout=0)

buffer = memoryview(bytearray(1024))

poller = select.poll()
poller.register(sys.stdin.buffer, select.POLLIN)

while True:
    for (s, event) in poller.ipoll(0):
        # There seems to be no way to do a non-blocking read of as many bytes as are currently available.
        # Instead, one must read a byte at a time (with `ipoll` telling you that at least one byte is available).
        read_count = s.readinto(buffer[:1])
        # ...
```

**3.** Creating a `machine.UART` instance (whether with a `baudrate` or other change or not) always results in a _harmless_ `E (738) uart: uart_wait_tx_done(1115): uart driver error`:

```
from machine import UART

UART(0)
```

---

Note: for reference, see [`machine_uart.c:366`](https://github.com/micropython/micropython/blob/f1d6af9/ports/esp32/machine_uart.c#L366) - one can see there's a special case for UART0 (i.e. `MICROPY_HW_UART_REPL` at this level) - it isn't deleted and recreated (but is later reconfigured by the code following this block):

```
if (uart_num != MICROPY_HW_UART_REPL)
//  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
{
    check_esp_err(uart_driver_delete(self->uart_num));

    check_esp_err(uart_param_config(self->uart_num, &uartcfg));

    check_esp_err(uart_driver_install(uart_num, self->rxbuf, self->txbuf, 0, NULL, 0));
}
```

comments.author: participant6
comments.body:
> This issue was not about the repl releasing control of UART 0. It was about changing the bit rate for UART 0.

Yes, I understand that. But to change the baud rate (or any other characteristic of the UART associated with the REPL), one creates a `machine.UART` instance that corresponds to UART0.

Given that it's done this way, one might naively assume that the constructed `machine.UART` instance would then be useable.

This does not seem to be the case. _Maybe_ adding a function into the `esp32` library would have been clearer, e.g. something like:

```
esp32.reconfigure_repl_uart(baudrate=9600)
```

This would avoid the creation of a `machine.UART` instance that confusingly turns out to be unusable, i.e. its sole purpose was to pass the constructor arguments down to the C layer in order to reconfigure the REPL UART and doing anything with the resulting instance (like calling `any()` or `write()`) will result in an error.

```python

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
if you provide me with a link to the board you are using I will be able to tell you if it is using the UART or USB-CDC for the connection. Then I can tel you what the best way to go about it is...

@participant10 

There is an easier way to handle the boot.py and needing to connect at 115200. You actually don't even need to bother with the boot.py anymore if you are using the latest release of MicroPython.

You can simply add `-DMICROPY_HW_UART_REPL_BAUD={speed}` to your build command. Replacing `{speed}` with the connection speed you want to use. When you do that the connection speed will always be the speed you provided. There is no need to switch back and forth between different UART speeds. This will only work if your ESP32 is using UART for the REPL.
